case_name: Aayush Prashant Agarwal v. Uma Exports Ltd. & Klass Insolvency Resolution Professionals Pvt. Ltd.
citation: 2026 LLBiz NCLAT 338; I.A. No. 5601 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1366 of 2024
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: Ruling on an appeal by the suspended director of Epic Yarns Private Limited (admitted into CIRP on an application by operational creditor Uma Exports Limited, with Klass Insolvency Resolution Professionals appointed IRP), the NCLAT set out a three-phase withdrawal framework under Section 12A of the IBC as substituted by the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026. Withdrawal is barred outright before the Committee of Creditors is constituted, permitted only with 90% CoC voting-share approval after CoC constitution and before the Resolution Professional issues the Form G invitation for resolution plans, and permanently barred once Form G has been issued, regardless of any settlement.
why_it_matters: Corporate debtors and creditors negotiating a settlement after a CIRP has commenced must now time their withdrawal application precisely around CoC constitution and the Form G invitation — missing either window closes off the settlement-exit route entirely under the tightened 2026 regime.

case_name: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha v. Tech Square Engineering Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
holding_summary: Reversing a 2023 Single Judge finding that Toyota had not proven Indian use or reputation in the mark ALPHARD predating Tech Square's 2015 'proposed to be used' registration, a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court held that unsolicited grey-market imports, online listings and press coverage since 2008 were sufficient to establish trans-border reputation in India. The Court declared ALPHARD a well-known trade mark and ordered cancellation of Tech Square's Indian registrations, holding that in luxury/niche markets brand visibility and global reputation — not mass local penetration — drive consumer recognition.
why_it_matters: Foreign brand owners without direct Indian sales now have a clearer, DHC-endorsed evidentiary path — grey-market presence, online visibility and press coverage — to establish trans-border reputation and defeat squatted registrations of niche or luxury marks in India.

case_name: D.P. Jain Bangalore Chennai Expressways Pvt. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India
holding_summary: Under a Concession Agreement dated 4 February 2022 for a section of the Bangalore-Chennai Expressway, a Division Bench had on 20 August 2026 partly allowed D.P. Jain's appeal, declaring the project eligible for free fly ash with transportation and referring its monetary claim (including Rs. 180.16 crore) to the Dispute Resolution Board/Arbitral Tribunal for quantification. After NHAI declined to implement that ruling and terminated the Concession Agreement on 1 September 2026, Justice Sachin Datta of the Delhi High Court, on 10 September 2026, constituted a three-member Arbitral Tribunal after both parties agreed to depart from the SAROD arbitration procedure prescribed in their agreement.
why_it_matters: Concessionaires facing an authority's non-implementation of a favourable court ruling, followed by termination of the concession, can secure a substitute tribunal by consent even where the contract mandates a specific institutional arbitration mechanism like SAROD.

case_name: Pr. Commissioner of Income Tax (Central)-2 v. M/S Delhivery Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: The Revenue had disallowed Delhivery's claimed deduction of Rs. 51.48 crore for ESOP expenditure and made an addition under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, on the ground that the share valuation supporting the ESOP had been prepared by a Chartered Accountant rather than a merchant banker. A Delhi High Court bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Rajneesh Kumar Gupta upheld the deduction, holding that a CBDT order permitted CA-prepared valuations at the relevant time and that a later rule requiring merchant-banker valuation could not be applied retrospectively to reject it.
why_it_matters: Companies that claimed ESOP expenditure deductions using contemporaneous Chartered Accountant valuations have a strong precedent to resist reassessment where the Revenue seeks to apply a later, stricter valuation-methodology requirement retrospectively.

case_name: MITC Rolling Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/S. Renuka Realtors & Ors.
holding_summary: MITC Rolling Mills had filed Commercial Suit No. 06 of 2021 before the District Judge, Nashik, seeking recovery of over Rs. 2.52 crore for supply of TMT/Fe-500 material; when its plaint was rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, the Bombay High Court held that no appeal lay against that order under Section 13(1A) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. The Supreme Court, per Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta, set that aside, holding that rejection of a plaint is a 'decree' under Section 2(2) CPC and is therefore appealable under the main part of Section 13(1A), with the proviso restricting only appeals against purely interlocutory orders.
why_it_matters: Commercial litigants whose plaint has been rejected under Order VII Rule 11 now have settled confirmation that a first appeal lies as of right under the Commercial Courts Act, removing an uncertainty that previously varied across High Courts.

case_name: Industria de Diseño Textil, S.A. v. Registrar of Trade Marks & Anr.
holding_summary: Inditex, owner of the ZARA mark, appealed the Trade Marks Registry's refusal to cancel a third party's registration of ZORA (Registration No. 4310686 in Class 24). Justice Jyoti Singh held that a mark need not first be formally declared 'well-known' under Section 11(6)-(9) before its owner can invoke the cross-category protection in Section 11(2) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and, applying the anti-dissection rule, found ZORA phonetically and structurally similar enough to ZARA that its adoption was without due cause and would take unfair advantage of ZARA's distinctive character and repute. The Court ordered cancellation of the ZORA registration and directed the Registrar to remove it from the Register within two months.
why_it_matters: Owners of globally recognised brands do not need a separate, formal 'well-known mark' declaration in hand before invoking Section 11(2) to block a similar mark in an unrelated goods category — reputation and distinctiveness evidence placed before the court can suffice on its own.

case_name: M/s Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Suryakand D. Lad & Ors.
holding_summary: Workers engaged through a contractor at ONGC claimed gratuity directly from ONGC as principal employer; the Controlling Authority under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 and, on appeal, the Bombay High Court had held ONGC liable to pay. A bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and Manmohan set that aside, holding that a Controlling Authority's jurisdiction under the Act is limited to computing the gratuity due to an already-established employee — it has no power to first adjudicate the disputed, anterior question of who the real employer is. Since ONGC had already paid the workers the disputed amount, the Court directed that no recovery be made from them.
why_it_matters: Principal employers facing a gratuity claim from contract workers should raise the employer-identity dispute at the earliest stage and be prepared to contest jurisdiction, since a Controlling Authority's order fixing them as the liable employer is now vulnerable to challenge as being outside its statutory power to decide.

case_name: Securities and Exchange Board of India v. Vedanta Limited & Ors.
holding_summary: Vedanta had announced a buyback of 17.09 crore equity shares at up to Rs. 335 per share but ultimately bought back only about 3.67 crore shares for Rs. 1,225.45 crore; SEBI alleged the announcement was misleading and made without genuine intent to complete it, invoking the PFUTP Regulations, while Vedanta argued SEBI's own release of its buyback escrow showed there was no fraud. A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan held that release of the cash escrow deposited under Regulation 15B(8) of the Buyback Regulations does not bar a separate, independent fraud inquiry under the PFUTP Regulations, but remanded the fraud question itself to the Securities Appellate Tribunal for fresh decision within six months, since neither the Adjudicating Officer nor SAT had engaged with disputed discrepancies in the underlying trading data.
why_it_matters: Companies cannot treat SEBI's release of a buyback escrow as closing the door on fraud scrutiny of the same buyback announcement — a PFUTP inquiry into the company's true intent at the time of announcement can proceed independently and on its own evidentiary track.
